overview: Burberry is a 170-year-old British luxury fashion house headquartered in London, best known for its trench coats, scarves and the Burberry Check, which it designs, manufactures and sells globally through directly operated stores, wholesale partners, licensees and e-commerce. The company is roughly two years into "Burberry Forward," a brand-and-cost turnaround led by CEO Joshua Schulman (since July 2024) after a multi-year period of profit warnings, inventory write-downs and management change under his predecessor. Burberry operates across four regions (EMEIA, Greater China, Americas, Asia Pacific) in the aspirational/mid-tier end of the global personal luxury goods market, below mega-brands such as Louis Vuitton, Gucci and Hermès.

business_model.summary: Burberry designs and sells luxury apparel and accessories, generating revenue primarily from directly operated retail (stores, concessions, outlets and Burberry.com), supplemented by wholesale sales to multibrand/department-store partners and licensing royalties (notably Coty for beauty/fragrance and an eyewear licensee). FY2025/26 revenue was £2,420m, flat at constant exchange rates after several years of decline; the business is working to rebuild from a low base following FY2024/25's inventory reset and profit collapse.

revenue_streams.name: Retail
revenue_streams.trend: stable/recovering (comparable sales +2% FY25/26, guided to continue improving)

revenue_streams.name: Wholesale
revenue_streams.trend: inflecting upward - declined ~4-5% in FY25/26 but FY27 guidance raised twice, now 10-12% CER growth

business_model.product_mix: Accessories ~35% of revenue (scarves and leathergoods, with scarves outperforming), Womenswear ~30%, Menswear ~29%, Childrenswear and other ~4%. Outerwear and scarves are the designated 'hero' categories under Burberry Forward and have outperformed the rest of the range throughout FY2025/26 and into FY2026/27.
business_model.customer_type: B2C, aspirational-to-top-tier luxury consumer, with Gen Z identified by management as the fastest-growing customer cohort; some B2B exposure via wholesale/department-store and franchise partners (413 directly operated stores plus 27 franchise stores as of mid-2026)
business_model.geographic_mix: EMEIA ~34% of FY25/26 revenue, Greater China ~28%, Americas ~21%, Asia Pacific ~15%. Greater China and the Americas drove the strongest recovery in FY25/26 (both up double-digit in Q4), while EMEIA has been held back by the Middle East conflict and weak tourist spending, and Japan has been hurt by declining Chinese inbound tourism.

main_competitors: Mulberry and Barbour (niche British heritage outerwear/accessories)
competitive_position.market_position: Mid-tier, aspirational luxury player, smaller than the mega-conglomerate houses (LVMH, Kering); Burberry is positioned as a specialist in British heritage outerwear and scarves rather than a full-range hard/soft luxury house. It lacks the scale, diversification and balance-sheet resilience of LVMH or Richemont, making it more exposed to a single-brand demand shock.

moat_factors.description: Thomas Burberry's 1856 origin, the Equestrian Knight Device (EKD/Prorsum), the Burberry Check and the trench coat are globally recognized house codes that differentiate Burberry from newer luxury entrants

Burberry Forward deliberately concentrates brand investment in outerwear and scarves (its historically strongest categories), which have outperformed the rest of the range and the wider luxury market for multiple consecutive quarters

Owns its gabardine mill in Keighley and trench coat factory in Castleford (undergoing a two-year renovation) plus leather goods/outerwear centres of excellence in Italy, supporting 'Made in Britain' authenticity but adding fixed cost relative to peers who outsource more broadly
Beauty/fragrance licensed to Coty and eyewear to a specialist licensee extends brand reach into accessible categories without full capital commitment, but licensing revenue has been declining

weaknesses: Materially smaller scale than LVMH/Kering/Richemont, limiting negotiating leverage with landlords, suppliers and media, and reducing resilience to a single-brand misstep

History of logo/monogram overexposure and inconsistent creative direction (multiple creative-director and CEO changes since 2017) diluted brand desirability and pricing power before the current turnaround
Heavier reliance on wholesale/department-store distribution than ultra-luxury peers, exposing revenue to the secular decline of that channel
Revenue still below the pre-pandemic/pre-slump base (£3bn target explicitly framed by management as a return to a prior level, not new territory) and well off FY2022/23 peak
No dividend currently paid, reducing the stock's appeal to income-oriented holders during the recovery phase

growth_drivers: "Burberry Forward" strategy (launched November 2024 under CEO Joshua Schulman) built on four pillars: Brand (Timeless British Luxury), Product (lead with outerwear), Distribution (align with product/customer strategy) and People (reignite high-performance culture)

Hero-product strategy concentrating marketing and merchandising on outerwear and scarves, supported by in-store 'Scarf Bars' (200+ rolled out in FY25/26) and new 'polo galleries'/trench destinations being rolled out in FY2026/27
Cost-reduction programme: £80m of annualised savings delivered in FY2025/26, targeting £100m annualised by FY2026/27, supporting margin recovery independent of a full revenue rebound

Wholesale re-acceleration: guidance for wholesale revenue growth has been raised twice during FY2026/27 (from mid-single-digit in May 2026 to high-single-digit in July 2026 to 10-12% CER growth at the November 2026 H1 results), reflecting a more positive reception from wholesale partners

Geographic reacceleration in Greater China and the Americas, both up double-digit in Q4 FY2025/26 and continuing into FY2026/27, as local (non-tourist) demand strengthens and Gen-Z customer acquisition grows
E-commerce investment (site-experience improvements) driving high-teens/mid-teens online growth

170th-anniversary brand activations (Portraits of an Icon campaign, Royal Collection Trust collaboration, Year of the Horse capsule) designed to reignite cultural relevance and attract new customers across cohorts
Executive Committee restructuring (new Chief Operating and Supply Chain Officer and Chief Customer Officer roles, Regional Presidents added) aimed at sharper, faster decision-making

business.risk: Execution risk on an unfinished turnaround
business.description: Burberry Forward has delivered two years of sequential improvement but revenue (£2,420m FY25/26) remains well below prior peaks and management's explicit £3bn medium-term target; analysts remain split on whether the recovery is durable into its harder second half

Company-identified principal risk: misalignment between inventory planning and consumer demand, driven by macro conditions, brand relevance, pricing architecture and competitive dynamics in a polarizing luxury market
Negative publicity, unethical behaviour or cultural missteps in campaigns/collaborations could damage brand equity in a business highly dependent on perceived luxury status
Failure to successfully deliver and sustain the benefits of Burberry Forward could leave the company underperforming luxury peers; this is an explicit Board-designated principal risk
Counterfeiting and parallel trade of a recognizable, heritage-coded brand (Check, EKD, trench silhouette) could erode exclusivity and pricing power

financial.description: Dividend suspended since FY2024/25; management has not committed to a reinstatement date, prioritizing reinvestment and balance-sheet strength, which weighs on total shareholder return in the interim

Net leverage improved to 1.6x by FY2025/26 year-end with borrowings down to £511m and cash of £614m; a new £300m revolving credit facility (maturing November 2031) was signed at the November 2026 H1 results, replacing a 2021 facility, but liquidity/cash fell to £459m by H1 FY2026/27 on continued investment

Significant translation and transaction exposure to USD, EUR, CNY, HKD, KRW and JPY; currency has swung between a revenue headwind and tailwind guidance update to update, adding volatility to reported results

regulatory.description: Carbon pricing, deforestation and supply-chain traceability regulation (e.g., EU-aligned disclosure requirements) could raise compliance costs; Burberry has pushed back a 100%-traceability target from a fixed 2030 date to a more flexible, risk-based commitment

Operating across 140+ countries exposes Burberry to a wide range of product, tax, trade, sanctions, anti-bribery and data regulations; a major compliance breach is a named principal risk, though currently assessed as low tolerance/well-controlled

macro.risk: China/Asia luxury demand softness and tourism flows
macro.description: Mainland China luxury spend declined 3-5% in calendar 2025 per Bain-Altagamma data; Japan has been hurt by declining inbound Chinese tourism; Greater China is Burberry's second-largest region and critical to the recovery narrative

Company-flagged increasing principal risk in FY2025/26; the Middle East conflict has directly weighed on EMEIA comparable sales (region declined in H2 FY25/26 and Q1 FY26/27) via reduced tourist spend and regional instability

Aspirational luxury demand (Burberry's core customer segment) is more cyclical than ultra-luxury/top-client spend; management repeatedly cites an 'uncertain geopolitical and macro-economic environment' in guidance

Exposure to cotton, wool, leather, viscose and synthetic material pricing and availability; mitigated partly by vertically integrated UK/Italy manufacturing but concentration in those sites is itself a supply-chain risk

macro_factors.industry_outlook: The global personal luxury goods market (Bain-Altagamma) was roughly flat at constant exchange rates in calendar 2025 (down ~2% at current rates) after a period of post-pandemic overheating and subsequent correction; the market is polarizing between resilient top-client/ultra-luxury spend and more price-sensitive aspirational demand, with value-for-money, outlet and pre-owned channels gaining share
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate-to-high - Burberry sits in the more discretionary, aspirational end of luxury, making it more cyclical than ultra-luxury houses (Hermès) and large diversified conglomerates (LVMH), but less cyclical than mass fashion retail
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Low direct, moderate indirect - rates affect Burberry's own financing costs and the broader consumer wealth/confidence backdrop (equity market wealth effects have been cited by management as supporting US demand)

recent_developments.event: H1 FY2026/27 interim results: revenue up ~6% to ~£1.09bn for the 26 weeks to 26 September 2026; adjusted operating profit rose to £62m from £19m a year earlier, a stronger-than-expected profit beat; shares jumped roughly 8% on the day. A new £300m revolving credit facility maturing November 2031 was signed, replacing a 2021 facility; cash (net of overdrafts) was £459m at period end, down from £614m at FY25/26 year-end reflecting continued investment. FY2026/27 wholesale revenue guidance raised again to 10-12% growth at CER

Mixed sell-side re-rating: RBC Capital downgraded to Hold (c.1,200p target, Sept 22) citing valuation after the rally, while Citi reiterated Buy with a 1,460p target (Sept 24); consensus skewed Buy (c.11 Buy/6 Hold/4 Sell of ~21 analysts) with average targets clustering roughly 1,250-1,360p versus a share price around 1,000-1,040p in September/October 2026

Q1 FY2026/27 trading update: comparable retail sales up 5%, with growth across Womenswear, Menswear, Accessories and Childrenswear for the first time in three years, led by Americas (+12%) and Greater China (+9%); EMEIA declined 3% on Middle East conflict and weak tourist spend. H1 FY27 wholesale guidance raised to high-single-digit growth. Shares nonetheless fell roughly 6% on the day as investors questioned the sustainability/pace of the recovery and flagged a ~37% shareholder vote against the CEO's new remuneration package at the 2026 AGM

FY2025/26 full-year results (52 weeks to 28 March 2026): revenue £2,420m (flat CER), adjusted operating profit £160m vs £26m prior year (+551% CER), adjusted diluted EPS 15.2p vs (14.8)p loss prior year, gross margin recovered 530bps CER to 67.9%, free cash flow £141m (+120%), leverage improved to 1.6x. Dividend remained suspended. Chair Gerry Murphy announced retirement effective the November 2026 interim results date, succeeded by William Jackson (joining the Board 1 July 2026)

Q3 FY2025/26 results presentation: comparable retail sales +3% (sequential improvement from Q2's +2%), driven by outerwear/scarves outperformance and Gen-Z customer growth in all regions; management guided FY2025/26 adjusted operating profit to be in line with consensus

items.notes: Raised from 'high-single-digit growth in H1 FY27' (July 2026 trading update) and from 'mid-single-digit growth in H1 FY27' (May 2026 full-year results), reflecting a progressively more positive response from wholesale partners
Consistent across May, July and November 2026 guidance updates

items.target: £100m annualised cost savings by FY2026/27 (of which £80m delivered in FY2025/26)
items.notes: FY2025/26 target of £80m was fully achieved
Down sharply from the ~£50m restructuring charge incurred in FY2025/26, implying the heavy-lift restructuring phase is largely complete
Consistent with FY2025/26 capex level; includes continued investment in the Castleford factory renovation
First introduced as explicit guidance at the May 2026 results

items.target: FX impact on revenue and adjusted operating profit has moved between a modest headwind and tailwind across successive updates
items.notes: May 2026 (at 1 May spot rates): ~£10m headwind to both revenue and adjusted operating profit. July 2026 (at 26 June spot rates): ~£20m tailwind to revenue, broadly neutral to adjusted operating profit. Guidance is explicitly rate-sensitive and liable to further revision

items.target: Revenue growth and margin expansion; long-term ambition to return to £3bn in annual sales
items.notes: Management repeatedly frames FY2026/27 as continued 'disciplined execution' of Burberry Forward while remaining 'mindful of the uncertain geopolitical and macro-economic environment'

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Joshua Schulman has progressively increased his public confidence through FY2026/27, citing 'momentum' and, at Q1 FY27, the first quarter of growth across all four product divisions in three years. The H1 FY27 results (profit more than tripling year-on-year) were characterized by analysts as 'another profit beat' keeping the turnaround on track, though some commentators and a meaningful minority of shareholders (c.37% opposed the CEO's new pay package at the July 2026 AGM) remain cautious about whether the recovery can be sustained through its harder second half, particularly given continued EMEIA weakness tied to the Middle East conflict and softer tourist spend.

bull_case: Clear, credible turnaround under CEO Joshua Schulman (Burberry Forward) delivering sequential improvement in comparable sales for seven consecutive quarters and a 551% CER increase in adjusted operating profit in FY2025/26, with H1 FY2026/27 profit more than tripling year-on-year

Repeated upward revisions to wholesale guidance (mid-single-digit to high-single-digit to 10-12% CER growth across three successive FY2026/27 updates) suggest demand momentum is building faster than initially planned, not just cost-cutting

Deep, globally recognized 170-year British heritage brand equity (trench coat, Check, EKD) provides a durable platform for re-engagement, now being focused deliberately on its strongest categories (outerwear, scarves) rather than diluted across the full range

£100m annualised cost-savings programme largely delivered with restructuring charges falling sharply (from ~£50m to ~£5m guided for FY2026/27), supporting structural margin expansion independent of further topline recovery

Improving balance sheet (leverage down to 1.6x, new £300m RCF through to 2031) gives the company runway to keep investing in brand and manufacturing (e.g., Castleford factory renovation) through the remainder of the turnaround
bear_case: Revenue (£2,420m FY2025/26) remains well below Burberry's prior peak and its own medium-term £3bn ambition; the easier, lower-base phase of the recovery may be largely behind it, with tougher comparisons ahead

EMEIA, Burberry's largest region by FY2025/26 revenue, has swung back into decline (H2 FY25/26 and Q1 FY26/27) due to the Middle East conflict and weak tourist spend, showing the recovery is uneven and exposed to factors outside management's control

Mainland China/Greater China luxury demand remains fragile at the industry level (Bain-Altagamma reported a 3-5% constant-currency decline in calendar 2025), and Burberry's recent regional outperformance could reverse if broader Chinese consumer sentiment weakens again

No dividend has been paid since FY2024/25 and management has given no reinstatement date, so total shareholder return depends entirely on share-price appreciation through an unproven, multi-year turnaround

Burberry remains structurally subscale next to LVMH, Kering and Richemont, with less resilience to a brand-specific misstep, less negotiating power with landlords/suppliers, and a smaller marketing budget to sustain cultural relevance against far larger, better-capitalized rivals

Shareholder friction is visible (c.37% opposed the CEO's new remuneration policy at the 2026 AGM), and the stock fell on the July 2026 trading update despite positive sales growth, indicating the market is pricing in a high bar for continued execution
